mean: to apply one rule to every case, ignoring differences
lit: to cut everything with one stroke of the knife, so every piece comes out the same

use.how: Used as a verb (不能一刀切, 搞一刀切), an adverb (一刀切地禁止) or before 的. Said of rules, policies and management that ignore real differences.

near.diff: 一视同仁 is praise for treating everyone equally and fairly; 一刀切 criticises a rule applied rigidly to cases that differ.
一概而论 is judging or talking about different things as if they were the same; 一刀切 is acting on them with one rule.

cue: The new rule says every employee must arrive at nine, whether they live next door or two hours away, and nobody can ask for an exception. What do the staff complain about?

ctx.s: 每个学生的情况都不一样，管理上不能{一刀切}。
ctx.en: Every student's situation is different, so you can't manage them all with one rule.

ctx.s: 公司要求所有人九点到岗，不管住多远，这种{一刀切}的做法引起了不满。
ctx.en: The company requires everyone to be at work by nine however far away they live, and this one-size-fits-all approach has caused resentment.

ctx.s: 小区突然禁止所有电动车进门，住户问：“这样{一刀切}，腿脚不好的老人怎么办？”
ctx.en: The estate suddenly banned all e-bikes from the gate, and residents asked: "If you ban them across the board, what about elderly people who can't walk well?"

ctx.s: 治理污染不能简单地{一刀切}，把所有小工厂都关掉。
ctx.en: Tackling pollution can't simply mean applying one blanket rule and shutting down every small factory.

ctx.s: 专家建议，孩子用手机应该按年龄管理，而不是{一刀切}地全面禁止。
ctx.en: Experts suggest that children's phone use should be managed by age rather than banned outright for everyone.

ctx.s: 新政策没有搞{一刀切}，而是给了各地一定的灵活性。
ctx.en: The new policy doesn't impose one rule on everyone; it gives each region some flexibility.

bad.s: 王老师对每个学生都{一刀切}，大家都很喜欢她。
bad.en: (meant: Ms Wang treats every student equally, and everyone likes her)
bad.why: It criticises a rigid rule that ignores differences; praise for treating people fairly and equally is yi shi tong ren.

bad.s: 他做事很{一刀切}，从来不拖泥带水。
bad.en: (meant: he is decisive and never dithers)
bad.why: It is not about being decisive; a person who acts quickly and cleanly is gan cui li luo (crisp and decisive).

mean: to rehash old material with nothing new added
lit: to stir-fry yesterday's cold rice and serve it up again

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often split (炒了不少冷饭). Said of films, songs, books, talks or ideas that serve up old content again as if it were new.

near.diff: 老生常谈 is a familiar, trite remark everyone has heard; 炒冷饭 is offering old work or content again as something new.
换汤不换药 is a change of name or form with no change in substance; 炒冷饭 is serving up the same old content again.

cue: A famous writer's "new" book turns out to be essays he already published years ago, put together again. What do readers say he is doing?

ctx.s: 这部电影又是{炒冷饭}，一点新意都没有。
ctx.en: This film is just a rehash again, with nothing fresh in it at all.

ctx.s: 新专辑里一半是老歌重新录的，粉丝说他在{炒冷饭}。
ctx.en: Half of the new album is old songs re-recorded, and fans say he is just recycling old material.

ctx.s: 老板看完方案说：“这些点子去年都用过了，别再{炒冷饭}了。”
ctx.en: After reading the proposal the boss said: "We used all these ideas last year, stop serving up the same old stuff."

ctx.s: 这本书不就是把他以前的文章重新编了一下吗？是不是在{炒冷饭}？
ctx.en: Isn't this book just his old articles re-edited? Isn't he simply rehashing old material?

ctx.s: 游戏公司这几年{炒了不少冷饭}，老游戏换个画面就重新卖。
ctx.en: In recent years the game company has done a lot of rehashing, putting new graphics on old games and selling them again.

ctx.s: 他的讲座每年内容都一样，学生们私下说他年年{炒冷饭}。
ctx.en: His lecture has the same content every year, and students say privately that he serves up the same old stuff year after year.

bad.s: 考试前我要把学过的课文{炒冷饭}，好好复习一遍。
bad.en: (meant: before the exam I'm going to go over the texts I've studied)
bad.why: Going over old lessons for yourself is fuxi (revise); this idiom criticises presenting old content to others as if it were new.

bad.s: 博物馆把这幅古画修复得跟原来一样，真是{炒冷饭}的好手艺。
bad.en: (meant: the museum restored the old painting perfectly, what fine craftsmanship)
bad.why: It is a criticism of stale repetition and cannot praise careful restoration of something old.

mean: a successful start right at the beginning
lit: red as the door opens: red, the colour of good fortune, on the very first day

use.how: A noun, usually after 取得, 实现, 迎来 or 来个: 新年开门红. Said of a good result at the start of a year, season, match series or new venture.

near.diff: 旗开得胜 is winning the very first battle or contest and is more bookish; 开门红 is a good start to a period such as a year, season or new business.

cue: On the first working day of the new year, your sales team closes the biggest deal it has had in months. How do you describe the start of the year?

ctx.s: 新年第一天就签了大单，真是{开门红}！
ctx.en: We signed a big deal on the very first day of the new year, what a great start!

ctx.s: 中国队首场比赛三比零获胜，取得了{开门红}。
ctx.en: The Chinese team won their first match three-nil, getting off to a winning start.

ctx.s: 新店开业第一天就排起了长队，老板笑着说这是个{开门红}。
ctx.en: On the new shop's opening day there was a long queue, and the owner said with a smile that it was a great start.

ctx.s: 朋友问他新工作怎么样，他说：“第一周就完成了两个项目，算是{开门红}吧。”
ctx.en: A friend asked how the new job was going, and he said: "I finished two projects in the first week, so it's off to a good start."

ctx.s: 今年一月份公司销售额大幅增长，实现了{开门红}。
ctx.en: The company's sales rose sharply this January, giving the year a strong start.

ctx.s: 新学期第一次考试，希望大家都能来个{开门红}。
ctx.en: It's the first test of the new term, and I hope everyone gets off to a flying start.

bad.s: 比赛最后一分钟他踢进了决胜球，真是{开门红}！
bad.en: (meant: he scored the winner in the last minute, what a finish!)
bad.why: It is only for a good result at the very beginning, never for a win at the end.

bad.s: 他一进门就害羞得满脸通红，真是{开门红}。
bad.en: (meant: he went red in the face with shyness as soon as he came in)
bad.why: It is a fixed phrase for a lucky good start, not a description of someone blushing at a door.

mean: everyone rushing to do the same thing at once
lit: a whole nest of bees pouring out together

use.how: Mostly used as an adverb (一窝蜂地挤进去, 一窝蜂似的) or before 的. Describes a crowd surging at once, and often mildly mocks everyone copying a trend.

near.diff: 蜂拥而至 is a written phrase that only describes crowds arriving; 一窝蜂 is colloquial and also mocks people all following the same trend.

cue: A few people made money opening bubble-tea shops, and suddenly everyone in town opened one too, so most went bust within a year. How did people rush into the business?

ctx.s: 下课铃一响，孩子们{一窝蜂}地跑向食堂。
ctx.en: As soon as the bell rang, the children all rushed off to the canteen at once.

ctx.s: 商场的门一开，顾客{一窝蜂}地挤了进去。
ctx.en: The moment the mall doors opened, the shoppers all crowded in together.

ctx.s: 前几年大家{一窝蜂}地去开奶茶店，现在很多都关门了。
ctx.en: A few years ago everyone rushed to open bubble-tea shops, and now many have closed down.

ctx.s: 选专业要看自己的兴趣，别看见什么热门就{一窝蜂}地去报。
ctx.en: Choose your major by your own interests; don't all pile into whatever is popular.

ctx.s: 听说超市鸡蛋打折，大爷大妈们{一窝蜂}似的赶了过去。
ctx.en: Hearing that the supermarket had eggs on sale, the old folks all swarmed over there at once.

ctx.s: 这种{一窝蜂}的投资方式风险很大，最后亏的往往是普通人。
ctx.en: This kind of herd investing is very risky, and it's usually ordinary people who end up losing.

bad.s: 他一个人{一窝蜂}地冲进了办公室。
bad.en: (meant: he rushed into the office on his own)
bad.why: It describes a whole crowd moving at once, so it cannot be said of one person.

bad.s: 我们组很团结，大家做事都{一窝蜂}，配合得特别好。
bad.en: (meant: our group is united and everyone works together really well)
bad.why: It pictures a disorderly crowd rushing or copying others, not well-coordinated teamwork, and is never praise.

mean: to suffer a humbling setback through a mistake
lit: to trip and fall flat, head over heels

use.how: An intransitive verb phrase, often split: 栽了个大跟头, 栽过跟头. Said of a person or company that fails through carelessness, pride or misjudgment.

near.diff: 碰钉子 is being flatly turned down when you ask for something; 栽跟头 is failing badly because of your own mistake.

cue: A star salesman who boasted he never needed to prepare lost the company's biggest client because he skipped the homework. What happened to him?

ctx.s: 他太骄傲了，早晚会{栽跟头}。
ctx.en: He is far too proud; sooner or later he'll come a cropper.

ctx.s: 这次考试我{栽了个大跟头}，数学没及格。
ctx.en: I really came unstuck in this exam: I failed maths.

ctx.s: 年轻人做生意{栽几个跟头}不要紧，关键是吸取教训。
ctx.en: It doesn't matter if young people take a few falls in business; what counts is learning the lesson.

ctx.s: 这家老牌公司就是因为忽视网上销售才{栽了跟头}。
ctx.en: This long-established company came to grief precisely because it ignored online sales.

ctx.s: 爸爸提醒他：“轻敌最容易{栽跟头}，比赛时认真点。”
ctx.en: His dad reminded him: "Underestimating your opponent is the easiest way to come a cropper, so take the match seriously."

ctx.s: 你在同一个问题上已经{栽过两次跟头}了，怎么还不长记性？
ctx.en: You've already been tripped up twice over the same thing; why haven't you learned?

bad.s: 今天出门被雨淋湿了，真是{栽跟头}。
bad.en: (meant: I got caught in the rain today, how unlucky)
bad.why: It is a real failure, usually from one's own mistake, not a small piece of bad luck like getting wet.

bad.s: 他在背后使坏，{栽跟头}了我。
bad.en: (meant: he worked against me behind my back and tripped me up)
bad.why: It is intransitive and cannot take a person as object; the one who fails must be the subject, as in rang wo zai le gen tou.

mean: to cause trouble through a careless blunder
lit: to poke a hole: jab at something and make a breach that others must patch

use.how: A verb-object phrase, often split: 捅了个大娄子, 捅出娄子, 他捅的娄子. Takes no object; said of someone whose blunder lands others in trouble.

near.diff: 闯祸 is the everyday word for causing an accident or trouble of any size; 捅娄子 is more colloquial and pictures a careless blunder that others must fix.
烂摊子 is the mess that is left behind; 捅娄子 is the act of causing the trouble.

cue: On their first day the new intern runs the wrong command and wipes half the client database, and now the whole team must stay late to fix it. What has the intern done?

ctx.s: 看你这副表情，是不是又{捅娄子}了？
ctx.en: Judging by that look on your face, have you gone and caused trouble again?

ctx.s: 他把合同上的价格写错了，{捅了个大娄子}。
ctx.en: He wrote the wrong price on the contract and landed us in big trouble.

ctx.s: 新来的实习生第一天就{捅了娄子}，把系统数据删了一半。
ctx.en: The new intern caused trouble on the very first day by deleting half of the system's data.

ctx.s: 你少说两句吧，别再{捅出什么娄子}来。
ctx.en: Say less, will you? Don't go stirring up any more trouble.

ctx.s: 妈妈出门前嘱咐：“在家老实待着，别给我{捅娄子}。”
ctx.en: Before going out, Mum said: "Behave yourself at home and don't get into any trouble."

ctx.s: 要不是经理及时发现，小王这回{捅的娄子}可就大了。
ctx.en: If the manager hadn't spotted it in time, the trouble Xiao Wang caused this time would have been serious.

bad.s: 他故意在背后{捅娄子}，想让同事丢掉工作。
bad.en: (meant: he deliberately sabotaged his colleague behind his back to get him fired)
bad.why: It is trouble caused by a careless blunder, not a deliberate plot against someone; that is shi huai (playing dirty).

bad.s: 小偷用刀{捅娄子}了他。
bad.en: (meant: the thief stabbed him with a knife)
bad.why: Tong alone means to stab; this idiom means causing trouble and cannot take a person as object.

mean: a mess left behind for someone else to sort out
lit: a broken-down, rotten market stall that someone has to take over

use.how: A noun, usually with 收拾, 接手, 留下 or 接: 收拾烂摊子. Said of a failing business, project or situation that someone else has to put right.

near.diff: 捅娄子 is the act of causing trouble; 烂摊子 is the messy situation left for someone else to deal with.

cue: Your predecessor quit suddenly, leaving unpaid bills, angry clients and missing records, and now it's all on your desk. What did they leave you?

ctx.s: 他说辞职就辞职，留下一个{烂摊子}给我。
ctx.en: He just quit out of the blue and left me with a mess to sort out.

ctx.s: 每次你闯了祸，都是我来收拾{烂摊子}。
ctx.en: Every time you get into trouble, I'm the one who has to clean up the mess.

ctx.s: 这个项目都快黄了，谁愿意接这个{烂摊子}？
ctx.en: This project is about to collapse; who would want to take over a mess like that?

ctx.s: 新经理接手的是一个{烂摊子}：欠债多，客户少，员工人心涣散。
ctx.en: The new manager inherited a mess: lots of debt, few customers and staff with no morale.

ctx.s: 同事抱怨：“前任把账目弄得一团糟，这种{烂摊子}谁都不想管。”
ctx.en: A colleague complained: "The last person made a total mess of the accounts, and nobody wants to deal with that kind of mess."

ctx.s: 老板退休后，女儿接下了工厂这个{烂摊子}，没想到三年就扭亏为盈了。
ctx.en: After the owner retired, the owner's daughter took over the failing factory and, surprisingly, turned it into a profit within three years.

bad.s: 他是个{烂摊子}，什么事都做不好。
bad.en: (meant: he is useless and can't do anything right)
bad.why: It is a messy situation left to others, not a word for a useless person.

bad.s: 对不起，我把公司的事{烂摊子}了。
bad.en: (meant: sorry, I messed up the company's business)
bad.why: It is a noun, not a verb; say gao za le (messed it up) or use it as an object of liu xia (left behind).

mean: a long-standing problem nobody has managed to solve
lit: old, big and hard: a problem that is long-standing, serious and difficult all at once

use.how: A noun or before 问题: 停车难是个老大难问题. Said of chronic problems in a city, workplace or community. It is also used of people who have long stayed single, but take care with that.

near.diff: 绊脚石 is anything or anyone that blocks progress; 老大难 is a problem that has dragged on for years without being solved.

cue: For twenty years residents of an old neighbourhood have complained there's nowhere to park, and every new committee promises to fix it but never does. What kind of problem is it?

ctx.s: 停车难是这个小区的{老大难}问题。
ctx.en: The lack of parking is this estate's long-standing problem.

ctx.s: 堵车一直是这座城市的{老大难}，修了地铁才好一点。
ctx.en: Traffic jams have long been this city's chronic problem, and things only got a bit better once the metro was built.

ctx.s: 老旧小区装电梯，为什么一直是个{老大难}？
ctx.en: Why has installing lifts in old housing estates remained such an intractable problem?

ctx.s: 经理在会上说：“客户投诉回复慢是我们部门多年的{老大难}，今年必须解决。”
ctx.en: The manager said at the meeting: "Slow replies to customer complaints have been our department's chronic problem for years, and this year we must fix it."

ctx.s: 新校长上任才三个月，就解决了食堂这个{老大难}。
ctx.en: Just three months after taking office, the new head teacher solved the canteen problem that had dragged on for years.

ctx.s: 村里的饮水问题拖了二十年，一直是个{老大难}，直到去年才通上自来水。
ctx.en: The village's water supply problem dragged on for twenty years, and only last year did running water finally arrive.

bad.s: 这道数学题太{老大难}了，我做不出来。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is too hard, I can't do it)
bad.why: It is a noun for a problem that has dragged on for years, not an adjective for something hard; a hard exercise is just hen nan (very hard).

bad.s: 他是我们公司的{老大难}，什么事都由他决定。
bad.en: (meant: he is the top boss of our company and decides everything)
bad.why: Laoda alone can mean boss, but this idiom is a chronic problem; the person in charge is yi ba shou.

mean: to fall out openly, dropping all pretence of goodwill
lit: to tear the face: rip away the polite mask people keep up with each other

use.how: A verb phrase, also 撕破脸皮 or split as 撕破了脸; often 跟某人撕破脸, 不想撕破脸. Said when two parties drop politeness and the conflict becomes open.

near.diff: 翻脸 is suddenly turning angry or hostile; 撕破脸 stresses that all politeness is gone and the conflict is now in the open.
闹别扭 is a passing sulk between people who are still close; 撕破脸 is an open break with no pretence left.

cue: For years two business partners stayed polite despite their quarrels, but now they insult each other in public and talk only through lawyers. What has happened between them?

ctx.s: 大家以后还要一起工作，别为这点小事{撕破脸}。
ctx.en: We all still have to work together, so don't fall out openly over something this small.

ctx.s: 为了遗产，兄弟俩最后{撕破了脸}，闹上了法庭。
ctx.en: Over the inheritance, the two brothers finally fell out openly and ended up in court.

ctx.s: 两家公司合作多年，这次因为合同纠纷彻底{撕破脸}了。
ctx.en: The two companies had worked together for years, but this contract dispute has turned them into open enemies.

ctx.s: 他欠钱一直不还，你还不好意思跟他{撕破脸}吗？
ctx.en: He has never paid back what he owes; are you still too embarrassed to have it out with him openly?

ctx.s: 她心里很不满，但表面上还客客气气的，不想跟对方{撕破脸}。
ctx.en: She was very unhappy inside, but stayed polite on the surface because she didn't want an open break.

ctx.s: 事情闹到{撕破脸}的地步，以后很难再合作了。
ctx.en: Now that things have come to an open break, it will be hard to work together again.

bad.s: 他在会上说错了话，觉得特别{撕破脸}。
bad.en: (meant: he said the wrong thing in the meeting and felt really humiliated)
bad.why: Feeling embarrassed is diu lian (lose face); this idiom is an open break between two parties, not a feeling.

bad.s: 小两口昨天为谁洗碗{撕破脸}了，今天早上就和好了。
bad.en: (meant: the young couple had a little spat about the dishes yesterday and made up this morning)
bad.why: It means a serious, open break in a relationship, not a small quarrel that is mended the next morning.

mean: to go to any length, even at great risk, to help a friend
lit: to have knives thrust into both sides of one's ribs for someone's sake

use.how: A verb phrase, usually 为朋友两肋插刀, or before 的 (两肋插刀的兄弟). Said of loyalty between friends that will take real risk or sacrifice.

near.diff: 雪中送炭 is timely help to someone in need; 两肋插刀 is loyalty so great that one would risk oneself for a friend.
赴汤蹈火 is braving any danger for a cause or a person and is more formal; 两肋插刀 is specifically loyalty to a friend.

cue: An old friend is in serious trouble, and you tell him you will stand by him even if it costs you your job and your savings. What are you ready to do for him?

ctx.s: 他是那种能为朋友{两肋插刀}的人。
ctx.en: He is the kind of man who would do anything, whatever the risk, for a friend.

ctx.s: 只要你一句话，兄弟我{两肋插刀}，在所不辞！
ctx.en: Just say the word, and I'll go through fire for you, no questions asked!

ctx.s: 当年他被人冤枉，只有老同学冒着得罪老板的风险站出来替他作证，这才叫{两肋插刀}。
ctx.en: When he was falsely accused back then, only an old classmate risked angering the boss to stand up and testify for him; that is what real loyalty to a friend looks like.

ctx.s: 嘴上说讲义气的人很多，可真遇到事，有几个肯{两肋插刀}？
ctx.en: Lots of people talk about loyalty, but when trouble really comes, how many will stick their neck out for you?

ctx.s: 为朋友{两肋插刀}是好事，但帮他做违法的事就不是义气了。
ctx.en: Going to any length for a friend is good, but helping him break the law is not loyalty.

ctx.s: 这部小说里的两个主人公是{两肋插刀}的好兄弟。
ctx.en: The two heroes of this novel are sworn friends who would risk anything for each other.

bad.s: 他对公司{两肋插刀}，十年来从来没迟到过。
bad.en: (meant: he is devoted to the company and hasn't been late once in ten years)
bad.why: It is loyalty between friends at great personal risk, not diligence or devotion to an employer.

bad.s: 同学忘带笔了，我{两肋插刀}借了他一支。
bad.en: (meant: a classmate forgot his pen, so I lent him one)
bad.why: It is for great risk or sacrifice; used for lending a pen it can only sound sarcastic.
